## 4. Review: "You Can See Everything" — Nathan Fielder's Documentary Shows Us Everything, Then Leaves Us Doubting Almost Everything We See

**Score:** 181
**Body:** You can see everything in "You Can See Everything," and you still may not believe everything you are seeing. And maybe you shouldn't? Is that the point of this hypnotic, totally surprising film?

It's already generating so much discussion, and rightfully so. And while some say they can't discuss the film without spoilers, here's my attempt at a SPOILER-FREE review (below, after the poster image).

My rating: \*\*\*\*½ of \*\*\*\*\*

￼​

"The rich are different from you and me."  
*— F. Scott Fitzgerald*

This can't be mere coincidence, can it? Less than three weeks into October, and the month has delivered three entirely different, extraordinary films that deal, in their own ways, with one of the foundational questions of existence: How do we know what we know? Can we really trust our eyes and ears?

The latest, following *Digger* and *La Bola Negra*, is the documentary *You Can See Everything* from Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, in which the often satirical, even-more-often ironic filmmakers make the most of the remarkable (and remarkably weird) opportunity to be flies on the wall in the last days before Elizabeth Holmes, the disgraced, convicted founder of Theranos, goes to prison for 12 years.

Theranos, you may recall, was the company that claimed it could run almost any diagnostic blood test off of one drop of blood. The story of the company and of odd, off-putting Holmes has been told before. *You Can See Anything* wastes precious little of is three-hour running time rehashing the story.

What it tries to understand is how Holmes let any of it happen, whether she was telling the truth at her trial, whether she really believed what she said, whether she deserved her prison sentence or is a victim herself — and, if so, of what or whom? Other people have done far worse and not gone to prison. It isn't hard to name them these days. But Holmes was different. Why?

It becomes clear right away in this mesmerizing, entirely unexpected documentary that Holmes is one of Fitzgerald's rich. She and her husband Billy Evans maintain over and over and over that Holmes never sold a single share, that money wasn't the goal for Holmes. It was for someone. But who? And how? And what if Holmes, with her unblinking doe eyes and her fixed smile, is lying? Or, even stranger, perhaps, what if she's telling the truth?

But the truth about what? The more Fielder, who is a constant on-camera presence, pushes Holmes, the more it seems she resists, even when she's acquiescing. This is an odd movie about an odd person. Holmes may not have been building Theranos for money, but she clearly has a lot of it. So do the people around her. It's just one of a thousand contradictions exposed, dissected, and turned inside-out in this film. These people *are different*, and this movie revels in this curiosity.

I could say "this *documentary*," but there are times when Fielder is aware that nothing in the film plays like a documentary. It's not even *designed* like a documentary. Can we believe those two shots? Can we trust every reaction shot? Should we take it as a matter of faith that cameras were everywhere, because they sure seem especially good at being in the right place at the right time.

The deeper Fielder gets into the story, and the closer Holmes comes to actually going to prison, the weirder, stranger and more complicated *You Can See Everything* gets. Fielder gets uncomfortably close to his subject. He seems to be everywhere, in a movie that is ostensibly a documentary and biography, and eventually we've got to ask if everything we're seeing is real. It seems to be, and yet it all seems ... convenient.

Then, when a traditional documentary would have been wrapping up, *You Can See Everything* does something that either solidifies its *documentary* classification or undermines it entirely. And everything about Holmes, her world, and her story becomes even stranger still. Evans turns into the movie's most loathsome figure (or is it character?), and almost every word out of his mouth seems to turn *You Can See Everything* back in on itself again.

It's all disorienting and captivating, unlike any documentary you've seen, and more akin to a psychological thriller in which the plot moves in byzantine ways.

By the end, it's hard to imagine that anyone who watches *You Can See Everything* will be neutral about Holmes. And there's every possibility that whatever opinion you came in with will have changed by the end of the movie. Not just your opinion about her, but about, well, almost everything.

\----  
You can also read this review or more of my movie writing at [www.thereinthedark.blogspot.com](http://www.thereinthedark.blogspot.com)

## 5. The Life of David Gale (2003)

**Score:** 152
**Body:** A forgotten, underrated crime drama-thriller, of which upon re-watching I have changed my tune about. Stars Kevin Spacey, Laura Linney and Kate Winslet.

Perhaps more relevant today than ever, examines capital punishment in the United States.

A gifted college academic (Spacey) and his close colleague (Linney) are staunch opponents of the death penalty and have lead an advocacy organisation that's generated national headlines for their protesting. However, the very person who vehemently detests capital punishment, suddenly finds himself on death row, accused of a brutal r\*pe and murder of one of his students. He requests new rising star magazine scribe (Winslet) to come out for an interview. And there the mystery and intrigue unfold.

I thought the three leads were all equally excellent and really propelled Winslet to serious drama (she'd finally win an Academy Award after several noms in 2008). Also shout-out to Gabrial Mann as Winslet's intern ("The Bourne Supremacy" & TV's "Revenge"), Matt Craven and the ever prolific at the time Rhona Mitra.

Well directed by Alan Parker (Oscar nominee "Midnight Express" and "Mississippi Burning"). Produced by Nicolas Cage (that was a surprise!) & his company Saturn Films and Alan Parker. Written by newcomer Charles Rudolph. Released by Universal.

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. A Therapist's Reflections on You Can See Everything

**Score:** 289
**Body:** Light Spoilers for You Can See Everything ahead - be forewarned!



It would be difficult to put onto the page all of the thoughts that have been crashing through my head since I saw “You Can See Everything” last night. But of course, the thing that has been keeping me up the most - literally keeping me up; it turns out the 10 PM showing was not the best for getting a good night’s sleep - is trying to wrap my head around the psychology of Elizabeth Holmes. I wanted to raise a few ideas here that especially stick out to me as a therapist with experience working with some very mentally ill people in my professional life.

To me, the scene that stuck out the most - that, in a way, feels like the closest thing the film has to a thesis statement - is when Nathan, in the first conversation he ever has with Elizabeth, brings up the magician David Blaine’s magic trick in which he seems to drive an ice pick directly through his hand. As Nathan explains to Elizabeth, people think it’s a trick, and that there must be some sort of smoke and mirrors. But the truth is that David Blaine has spent years hollowing out a small hole in his hand for just this purpose. The trick is that there’s no trick.

In much of the discussion of this film that I’ve seen (as well as the discussion of Holmes in the documentary itself!), it seems like people really, really want to believe that the Elizabeth Holmes we see is an intentional manipulation, that she, just like David Blaine’s ice pick, is smoke and mirrors. Firstly, I think this interpretation is natural: many of the lies that we encounter from others, or that we ourselves tell, are knowingly told for personal gain. But beyond that, I think there is something almost comforting in believing that Holmes is some sort of chess master-like expert of deceit. In every episode of Scooby-Doo, we feel relief when what appeared to be a monster is unmasked to be nothing more than a normal person with banal, explainable motivations. It is a comfort to think that Holmes is a rational person, acting knowingly (though immorally) in her own best interest, just as we want to see ourselves as rational, self-aware people.

However, I think the film challenges us to consider another possibility. What if the trick is that there is no trick? What if the ice pick really is going through David Blaine’s hand? And, to add my own analogy, what if, instead of being a Scooby-Doo monster, with a rational actor underneath just waiting to be unmasked, Elizabeth Holmes is nothing more than a mouse in a maze who has unthinkingly learned the best way to get to the cheese? 

That may sound harsh to Elizabeth Holmes, but I don’t mean it to be. There may be ways that all of us fit that mouse in a maze description. To explain what I mean, I want to take a slight detour into my work as a therapist. I currently work at a mental health treatment center for individuals with severe mental health disorders. As I watched the film, I more and more began to connect Holmes’s behavior in the movie with my experience working with individuals diagnosed with personality disorders. Many personality disorders - Borderline Personality Disorder, Avoidant Personality Disorder, Narcissistic Personality Disorder, Antisocial Personality Disorder - can include deceitfulness or manipulative tendencies as part of their presentation. And while this deceit can sometimes be the intentional kind of lies that we’re used to, it would be missing the mark to say that it always is.

Let me illustrate this with an example. At our treatment center, we worked with a client with a serious trauma history who ended up being diagnosed with Borderline Personality Disorder. One of this client’s core problems was that she was pathologically dependent on others and completely avoidant of ever taking ownership over her life. This manifested in some truly remarkable ways. Despite seeing many, many medical professionals who failed to find any diagnosable issue, this client suffered from frequent seizures, which could manifest as her fully falling out of her chair and writhing on the floor for minutes. These seizures predominantly happened when others were around, and seemed to increase as expectations in her life became unmanageable for her. At other times, this client claimed to hear voices, to have multiple personalities, or to suffer from various other medical ailments, though all of these behaviors lessened when they didn't result in attention from others or in someone else stepping in to take care of her.

Was this client lying? It depends on what your understanding of the word “lying” means, as Nathan and Elizabeth discuss at one point in the film. It is almost undeniable that this client was not “really” suffering from much of what she claimed to, and that these behaviors came from a desire to manipulate others to get outcomes she wanted (attention, care, reduced responsibilities). But I have to tell you, the longer I knew this client, the more it seemed to me that she was completely, perfectly convinced that everything she described was real. She was no Scooby-Doo monster, and there was no mask - this was “her truth”, to quote Holmes. As opposed to intentional lying, this client seemed to have learned that acting in these ways could manipulate outcomes in her favor, despite the fact that she was *completely consciously unaware* that manipulation was the intended function of her actions. Over the years, these behaviors became more and more reinforced, just as a mouse learns to navigate a maze to get a reward without ever understanding what it is doing, what a maze is, or that it is even in one.

In the simplest possible terms, one doesn’t have to understand why they do a behavior in order to do it, and benefit from it. And, while “You Can See Everything” argues convincingly that we can never know the truth about Elizabeth Holmes, it is at least worth considering the possibility that Holmes herself does not understand the full extent of her own manipulation, even if manipulation is the intended effect of her actions. Consider what we see in the documentary: Holmes seems to have her head in the clouds, to “not care about money,” to operate on a different wavelength far removed from the earthly concerns of most, even while she also has a knack for placing herself in romantic and business partnerships with men (first Sunny Balwani, then Billy Evans) who care a great deal about money. Consider, too, how well this works for Holmes: Billy Evans negotiates to ensure that they will get paid for their participation in the documentary, and yet Holmes has complete plausible deniability when confronted about this by Nathan, and can maintain her “creative visionary” persona even while she profits from her husband’s actions. Indeed, it was precisely this dynamic (with her prior partner Sunny) that led to Theranos’s success in the first place. Even just the fact that Holmes appears to so effectively win over Nathan, and by extension the viewer, is a result of her strange, disarming presence. But are Holmes’s persona and actions an intentional manipulation, or is it simply how she's learned to act because it gets the best results? What if, when Holmes claims over and over again that she has no idea what happened or how she could have arrived at this point, we believed her? 

For me, the brilliance of “You Can See Everything” is the extent to which it calls into question not just whether any of us can see into the hearts of others, but how much we even struggle to see what is within ourselves. Because, of course, it is not just Holmes who may do things without understanding why; all of us have layers of unconscious drives that dictate what we do more than we may care to admit. It’s worth wondering what mazes we've been running through, and what we've been running toward, without ever stopping to notice. 

### Top 5 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Yes! My father was not formally diagnosed unfortunately but he exhibited a lot of these same behaviors. It took me a long time to realize he wasn't actuallt consciously manipulating people most of the time exactlt, and he absolutely wasn't some mastermind, he was mostly just responding authentically and spontaneously based on habit and instinct in order to secure his immediate term desires without much if any regard or concern for truth or reality. I drove myself up the wall for years before realizing this, trying to figure out what he 'really' thought, trying to rationalize how he could possibly believe what he was saying etc. Ultimately 'a rat in a maze' is pretty close to how I came to understand his behavior.
2. I think these are fine reflections based on what is explicitly shown in the film but respectfully, how familiar are you with the actual Theranos case? Elizabeth engaged in many different, egregious, and specific forms of deceit and fraud, like forging pharmaceutical logos on reports and memos given to investors, lying about financial projections, staging fraudulent lab tests, among many others, all seemingly for commercial and financial gain. Far and above a simple intentional vague wording of the capabilities of the machine or trying to claim that she doesn't care about money. 

People can outwardly say and claim any number of things, but it's more instructive to see how their behaviors line up to start to see whether they're being truthful or not. And her actions do not at all point to someone who is "above" the money or "doesn't care about it". Why does she have complete plausible deniability? Why are we letting her off the hook? Because she's outwardly trying to claim she doesn't care? What do her actual and specific actions tell us? 

Much of the discourse around this film I fear suffers from a lack of context. If one was to only watch this film without any of the surrounding context you might leave this film fully sympathetic for Elizabeth. And I think the fact that this is a documentary adds another level of apparent trustworthiness. But do you have the full picture? What scenes didn't make it out of the editing room? Elizabeth had literal years to prepare for something like this documentary too, if she was successful in convincing so many others of her lies, is she being successful in this film too? Just like those investors, they didn't have the context of the deceitful actions Elizabeth took in preparing for those meetings. They didn't know she had photoshopped those pharmaceutical logos on there. If they were to just take a surface read of what was presented to them (which they seemed to have done), what conclusion did they draw? ## 5. My 60th anniversary reflection on Persona (1966).

**Score:** 8
**Body:** Ingmar Bergman’s Swedish classic *Persona* premiered 60 years ago today, on October 18, 1966.

Going into this review I would first like to preface that I do not fully understand this film. But… I also do not believe anybody truly does. “Persona” is a film with no direct explanation or reasoning for the events that are depicted throughout its runtime. Parts of the film seem somewhat random, out of place, and overtly radical such as the opening projector montage. Although that montage doesn’t make much sense I think it’s truly brilliant and one of my favorite opening scenes of all time. It’s random, intense, and made me feel deeply disturbed, setting the tone of the film perfectly.

The film focuses on the story of a nurse named Alma (Bibi Andersson) taking care of an intentionally mute patient named Elisabet Vogler (Liv Ullmann) in an isolated seaside cottage. Throughout that loosely told story are several central themes such as identity, public mask vs. private self, grief, guilt and the burden of creation. All of those themes are roughly introduced in the somewhat random prologue with the projector and carry on throughout the primary story with Alma and Elisabet. Although the crucifixion, spider, killing of a lamb and a boy waking up in a hospital and seeing a wall with two blurry women on it seem unrelated to the overall story of the film it serves as a brilliant introduction to the tone and some of the general themes the film covers. “Persona” is a perfect example of how art doesn’t have to be fully understood to be enjoyed.

I was extremely fond of how Ingmar Bergman depicted themes of identity in this film. Towards the start of the film (before they go to the cottage) Alma and Elisabet are in a hospital room and Elisabet tears up a photo of her son. Later on in the film (at the cottage), Alma finds Elisabet’s husband outside calling for Elisabet. She greets him and takes advantage of him mistaking her for Elisabet and sleeps with him. After that interaction, Alma confronts Elisabet about why she tore up the photo of her son at the start of the film and starts to tell the story of Elisabet’s life for her and how after a failed abortion she gave birth to a boy whom she despises, but who craves her love. Right after those scenes is an iconic composite shot of each of their faces forming a single head. Sven Nykvist’s cinematography really stands out here. By utilizing an extreme close-up for the faces merging together Nykvist creates an intimate and claustrophobic atmosphere reflecting the psychological erosion.

 Through describing Alma taking on the “persona” of Elisabet, pretending to be her, and a literal shot of their faces molding together, Bergman shows how these identities we display to the public are maintained only through distance, and through minimizing that distance the personality differences shatter as well. It shows how we as human beings are porous vessels and are immensely affected by the desires, judgements and personalities of the people that surround us. 

“Persona” has a very unique sense of isolation, paralysis, and physical disintegration which I think are the result of Ingmar Bergman’s personal crisis at the time. While writing “Persona,” Ingmar Bergman was hospitalized with severe vertigo and depression. Throughout the film, you can see how Bergman’s psychological troubles at the time are reflected in the two lead characters, each having their own mental struggles. I believe that Ingmar Bergman’s hospitalization interrupting him when he was at the peak of his career directly influenced his decision to have Elisabet Vogler go intentionally mute during a huge stage production.

“Persona” is by no means a story that anyone can fully grasp. It’s riddled with various details and aspects that are never explained, and that’s not particularly a bad thing. The film ends with Alma leaving the cottage, a film crew capturing her, the boy in the opening montage being shown once more and the projector from the beginning coming to a halt. I believe that the intent of Ingmar Bergman showing the film crew was to strip the film of its own mask, breaking down the fourth wall. Obviously, there are people who are sure to disagree and interpret it differently but that’s the beauty of ambiguity; everybody has their own interpretation. “Persona’s” inability to be dumbed down to a single explanation is a testament to its brilliance.

I think part of why this film is so important today is because it covers the harsh reality of the difference between our public and private selves which is even more relevant in the digital age where we can all carefully curate a digital persona of how we will be perceived.
